intro: Set a needle in the groove of a spinning record and a voice fills the room. Flip a switch and light crosses the room faster than you can blink. Tap send on a phone and a picture of Lake Michigan reaches a cousin in another state in about a second. None of these carry any stuff from one place to the other. The record stays on the turntable, the bulb stays in the ceiling, the phone stays in your hand. What travels is a pattern: a wave.

This unit is about waves and what they can carry. You will start with ripples on the wave bench and drums on the drum bench, learning to measure amplitude, wavelength and frequency. You will follow sound through air, water and steel into the ear, and light through glass and water into the eye. Then you will see how people turned those same waves into instruments: the microscope that showed Hooke his cells, the telescope that showed Galileo four moons, the radio, the fiber cable and the weather radar that warns of a tornado.

By the end you should be able to explain why sound goes silent in a vacuum while light does not, why a pencil looks bent in water, how two lenses make a microscope, why a digital photo survives a noisy connection when a record groove cannot, and how a bat, a submarine and a weather station all use the same trick of timing an echo.
bigQuestion: How do waves carry energy and information, and how have people learned to use them to see, hear and communicate beyond the reach of their own senses?

timeline.t: Galileo turns a two-lens spyglass on Jupiter and finds four moons circling it
Robert Boyle pumps the air from a jar and shows sound needs a medium
Robert Hooke publishes microscope drawings of cork and names the cell
Isaac Newton builds a telescope that gathers light with a mirror instead of a lens
Ole Roemer uses eclipses of Jupiter's moon Io to show that light has a finite speed
William Herschel finds invisible infrared light beyond the red end of a spectrum
Thomas Edison records and plays back a voice from a groove on a tinfoil cylinder
Heinrich Hertz makes and detects radio waves in his laboratory
Wilhelm Röntgen discovers X-rays and photographs the bones of a hand
The 40-inch Yerkes refractor opens in Wisconsin, the largest lens telescope ever used
The Hubble Space Telescope is launched above the blurring atmosphere
The James Webb Space Telescope launches to see the universe in infrared

words.d: a repeating disturbance that carries energy from one place to another without carrying the medium
how far the medium moves from rest; larger amplitude means more energy
the distance from one crest of a wave to the next
the number of complete waves passing a point each second, measured in hertz
the material a mechanical wave travels through, such as air, water or steel
a wave, such as sound, that needs a medium to travel
a wave of electric and magnetic fields, such as light, that needs no medium
the bending of light as it changes speed entering a new material
a curved piece of clear material that refracts light to focus or magnify it
the full range of electromagnetic waves from radio to gamma rays
a signal made of numbers stored as ones and zeros, which resists noise and copies exactly
a reflected wave whose delay tells how far away the reflecting object is

test.q: A ripple crosses a pond and passes a floating leaf. What does the leaf mainly do?
choices: Travels with the ripple to the shore
Bobs up and down and stays nearly in place
test.why: Waves carry energy, not the medium. The leaf rises and falls as the ripple passes but does not travel with it.

test.q: Which pair of changes would make a sound both louder and higher in pitch?
test.why: Loudness comes from amplitude and pitch from frequency. Louder and higher means larger amplitude and higher frequency.

test.q: A wave on the bench has frequency 3 Hz and wavelength 0.5 m. What is its speed?
test.why: Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength: 3 times 0.5 is 1.5 meters per second.

test.q: Why can a bell not be heard inside a jar with the air pumped out?
choices: Sound needs a medium, and there are no particles to carry the vibration
The bell stops ringing without air
The vacuum makes the sound too fast to hear
test.why: Sound is a mechanical wave. With no particles to push, the vibration of the bell cannot reach the glass.

test.q: In which medium does sound travel fastest?
choices: Sound travels at the same speed in all three
test.why: Tightly packed, stiffly bonded particles pass pushes along quickly. Sound moves about 6,000 m/s in steel, 1,480 in water and 343 in air.

test.q: Where in the ear do vibrations become nerve signals?
test.why: Hair cells along the membrane inside the fluid-filled cochlea fire nerve signals when their part of the membrane moves.

test.q: Why can sunlight cross space to reach Earth?
choices: Space is full of thin air
The sun pushes the light with solar wind
Light is an electromagnetic wave and needs no medium
test.why: Unlike sound, light carries its own electric and magnetic fields and travels through a vacuum at about 300,000 km/s.

test.q: A red apple looks red because it:
choices: Reflects red light and absorbs most other colors
test.why: We see the light an object sends back. The apple reflects red wavelengths and absorbs most of the green and blue.

test.q: What directly causes light to bend when it enters water from air?
choices: Light changes speed at the surface
Light changes color at the surface
test.why: Light slows down in water. At an angle, the change in speed swings the beam, which is refraction.

test.q: A student sees distant signs as a blur but reads a book easily. Which lens fixes this?
choices: A convex lens, thicker in the middle
A concave lens, thinner in the middle
test.why: She is nearsighted: light focuses in front of the retina. A concave lens spreads the rays so the focus lands on the retina.

test.q: A microscope with a 10x objective and a 20x eyepiece magnifies:
test.why: The eyepiece magnifies the image the objective already made, so the two multiply: 10 times 20 is 200.

test.q: Why are the biggest telescopes built with mirrors rather than lenses?
choices: A mirror can be supported from behind and made very large without sagging
Mirrors do not need to be pointed at the sky
test.why: A lens is held only at its edge and bends under its own weight past about a meter. A mirror can be huge.

test.q: Which electromagnetic wave has the highest frequency and the most energy per wave?
test.why: Shorter wavelength means higher frequency and more energy. X-rays are far shorter than visible, infrared or radio waves.

test.q: Why does a digital copy of a song stay perfect while an analog tape copy gains hiss?
choices: Digital signals travel by light only
Digital bits are read as ones and zeros, so small noise is discarded instead of copied
test.why: Noise added to an analog shape becomes part of the shape. Noise added to a bit is ignored as long as high and low can still be told apart.

test.q: A sonar ping in seawater, about 1,500 m/s, returns after 4 seconds. How deep is the bottom?
test.why: The round trip is 1,500 times 4, or 6,000 meters. The sound went down and back, so the depth is half: 3,000 meters.

write.prompt: Make a claim: Is a digital signal or an analog signal the better way to store and send a recording of a song? Support it with evidence from this unit about waves, noise, copying and the way a phone sends a picture, and explain your reasoning.
tips: State your claim in one clear sentence at the start.
Use at least two pieces of evidence: how noise affects a record groove or tape, how bits survive a noisy connection, and how sample rate limits what a digital file keeps.
Explain the reasoning: say why each piece of evidence supports your claim, using the words amplitude, noise and bit.
Give the other side a fair hearing: what does the losing choice do well, and when might someone prefer it?

title: Waves and Information

chapters.title: Waves, Sound and Light
chapters.bigQuestion: How can a wiggle in a groove, a push of air or a beam of light carry a song, a voice or a picture across a room?

story.title: The Groove That Sings
story.kicker: Put a record under a magnifying glass and you can see sound before you hear it.
paragraphs: A black vinyl record spins on the turntable at 33 and one-third turns each minute. A thin needle rests in a groove that spirals from the outer edge toward the center. To the eye the groove looks like a smooth line. Put a magnifying glass over it and the line breaks apart. It wiggles. It swings left and right, sometimes in wide sweeps, sometimes in tiny jitters packed close together.

Those wiggles are not decoration. They are a drawing of sound. When the record was made, a singer's voice shook the air, the air shook a microphone, and a cutting tool carved every shake into a spiral. Now the needle rides the groove, shakes the same way, and turns each shake into a small electric signal. The speaker pushes the air, and the room hears a voice that was recorded decades ago.

Look closer and you can read the music. A loud drum hit makes the groove swing wide; a soft hum keeps it narrow. A high whistle makes tight, fast wiggles; a low bass note makes long, slow ones. Width and spacing are the two things that matter, and in this chapter they get names: amplitude and wavelength.

Sound, water ripples, a shaking rope and light all share this shape. They are waves, patterns that carry energy from one place to another without carrying the stuff itself. The needle does not travel to the singer. The groove stays on the record. Only the pattern moves, and the pattern is enough to bring the song back to life.
story.think: If you could see the groove for a whisper and the groove for a shout side by side, how would they look different, and why?

lessons.title: Energy Moves, the Stuff Stays
lessons.mainIdea: A wave carries energy from place to place, but the material it travels through only moves back and forth.
reading: Drop a pebble into a still pond. Rings spread out from the splash. A leaf floating nearby bobs up and down, but it does not ride the ring to the shore. It ends up almost where it started. The ring moved. The water and the leaf did not go with it. That is the strange and useful thing about a *wave*: the pattern travels, the material does not.

A wave is a repeating disturbance that carries *energy* from one place to another. Stretch a rope along the floor and snap one end up and down. A hump runs down the rope. Each piece of rope only rises and falls, yet the hump reaches the far end and can knock over a cup there. The rope stayed put; the energy arrived.

Sound works the same way. A drum skin pushes the air next to it. That air pushes the air next to it, and so on. The air near the drum never travels to your ear. It just shoves its neighbors. What reaches you is a chain of pushes, and your eardrum feels the energy of the last push in line. Scientists call the material a wave moves through the *medium*: water for ripples, rope for the hump, air for sound.

words.d: a repeating disturbance that carries energy from one place to another
the ability to make something move or change
the material a wave travels through, such as air, water or a rope

look.title: The Stadium Wave
look.text: Picture a crowd doing the wave at a Chicago ballpark. Each person stands up, throws their arms in the air, and sits back down. The wave races all the way around the stadium in about half a minute. Nobody leaves their seat.
look.prompt: What moved around the stadium, and what stayed put? How is this like a ripple on a pond?

check.q: A leaf floats on a pond when a ripple passes. What does the leaf do?
choices: Bobs up and down and stays near the same spot
Rides the ripple to the shore
Sinks because the wave pushes it under
check.why: A wave carries energy, not the water. The leaf rises and falls as the ripple passes but stays close to where it was.

check.q: What does a wave carry from one place to another?
check.why: A wave is a traveling pattern of energy. The medium moves back and forth in place while the energy travels through it.

check.q: A drum is hit across a gym. Which best describes how the sound reaches you?
choices: Air from the drum flies to your ear
The drum skin stretches across the gym
A chain of pushes passes from air to air until it reaches your ear
Your ear pulls the sound toward it
check.why: Each bit of air shoves its neighbor. The pushes travel across the room even though no single bit of air makes the trip.

lessons.title: Amplitude, Wavelength, Frequency
lessons.mainIdea: Amplitude tells how much energy a wave carries, wavelength is the distance between repeats, and frequency is how many repeats pass each second.
reading: Every wave can be measured in three ways. *Amplitude* is how far the medium moves from its rest position, the height of a water hump above the flat surface or how far a rope swings from the middle. Bigger amplitude means more energy. On the turntable, a loud drum hit cut a wide swing in the groove; a whisper cut a narrow one. Doubling the amplitude of a wave does not just double its energy. It roughly quadruples it, which is why a shout can rattle a window when a normal voice cannot.

*Wavelength* is the distance from one crest to the next crest, or from one groove wiggle to the next matching wiggle. Long ocean swells might be 100 meters from crest to crest. The ripples in a bathtub are a few centimeters. *Frequency* is a different measure: it counts how many complete waves pass a point in one second. The unit is the *hertz* (Hz). A rope shaken twice a second makes a 2 Hz wave.

Wavelength and frequency are linked. If the wave speed stays the same, more waves per second must be packed closer together. So high frequency goes with short wavelength, and low frequency goes with long wavelength. For sound, frequency is what we hear as pitch: a bass note is low frequency, a whistle is high. For the eye, amplitude shows up as brightness and frequency as color, an idea this chapter returns to later.

words.d: how far the medium moves from its rest position; larger amplitude means more energy
the distance from one crest of a wave to the next
the number of complete waves that pass a point each second
the unit of frequency; one hertz is one wave per second

look.title: Frequencies of Some Sounds
rows: Upper limit of young human hearing
look.prompt: Which of these sounds has the shortest wavelength in air? How do you know without measuring?

check.q: Which change to a wave would make it carry the most extra energy?
check.why: Amplitude measures how far the medium moves. More amplitude means more energy, and doubling it roughly quadruples the energy.

check.q: A rope is shaken so that 5 complete waves pass a point every second. What is the frequency?
check.why: Frequency counts complete waves per second, measured in hertz. Five waves each second is 5 Hz.

check.q: Two sound waves travel through the same air at the same speed. One has a higher frequency. What must be true?
check.why: At the same speed, more waves per second must fit closer together. Higher frequency means shorter wavelength. Loudness is a separate thing, amplitude.

lessons.title: Reading the Wave Bench
lessons.mainIdea: Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength, so measuring any two of them tells you the third.
reading: The site's wave bench is a long tray of water with a paddle at one end. Set the paddle to move slowly and long, lazy ripples roll down the tray. Speed it up and the ripples get tighter and closer together, yet a marker floating in the tray shows each crest still takes the same time to travel the length of the bench. The speed of the ripples did not change. Only the spacing did.

This is a rule you can trust for any wave: *wave speed* equals frequency times wavelength. Say the paddle makes 2 waves per second and the crests are 0.5 meters apart. Then the crests travel 2 times 0.5, or 1 meter every second. Now double the frequency to 4 Hz. The water has not changed, so the speed is still 1 meter per second. That means the wavelength must shrink to 0.25 meters.

The rule matters because speed depends on the medium, not on the wave. Water of a certain depth carries ripples at one speed. Air at room temperature carries sound at one speed. So when a musician plays a higher note, the sound does not go faster; its wavelength gets shorter. On the turntable, the same idea appears as wiggles packed more tightly in the groove for the high notes, even though the record spins at a fixed rate.

You can use the rule on your own. Count how many ripples pass a mark in ten seconds, divide by ten to get frequency, then measure the crest-to-crest distance with a ruler. Multiply, and you have the wave speed of the bench without ever timing a single ripple.

words.d: how fast a crest travels through the medium; equal to frequency times wavelength
the highest point of a wave

look.title: Two Settings on the Paddle
look.text: On the wave bench, a student sets the paddle to 1 wave per second and measures the crests 30 centimeters apart. She then turns the paddle up to 3 waves per second. The water is the same depth. She measures again and finds the crests 10 centimeters apart.
look.prompt: What was the wave speed at each setting? What does that tell you about what controls wave speed?

check.q: A wave has a frequency of 4 Hz and a wavelength of 2 meters. How fast does it travel?
check.why: Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength: 4 times 2 is 8 meters per second.

check.q: What mainly decides how fast a wave travels?
choices: How hard the source was hit
check.why: Speed depends on the medium. Changing the frequency changes the wavelength, not the speed, as long as the medium stays the same.

check.q: A flute plays a higher note. Compared with the lower note, the sound wave in the air has:
choices: A shorter wavelength and the same speed
A longer wavelength and a faster speed
The same wavelength and a faster speed
A shorter wavelength and a slower speed
check.why: The air is the same, so the speed is the same. A higher frequency must mean a shorter wavelength.

lessons.title: Sound Needs Something to Push
lessons.mainIdea: Sound is a mechanical wave: it travels only by pushing through a medium, so it cannot cross empty space.
reading: Around 1660 the English scientist Robert Boyle hung a ringing watch inside a glass jar and pumped the air out. As the air thinned, the ticking faded. With most of the air gone, he could see the watch working but could not hear it. Let the air back in and the sound returned. Boyle had shown that sound needs a *medium*. Nothing in the jar was able to carry the pushes to the glass.

Sound is a *mechanical wave*, a wave that moves by shoving particles of matter into each other. A vibrating guitar string squeezes the air on one side, then the other, hundreds of times each second. Each squeeze is a region of slightly higher pressure, and each pull-back is a region of slightly lower pressure. These squeezes travel outward as a *compression* wave. In a *vacuum*, a space with no particles, there is nothing to squeeze, and sound simply stops.

This is why films that show roaring explosions in space are wrong. An astronaut outside the International Space Station hears nothing through the vacuum. Inside a suit, a radio carries voices, because radio is not sound. It is a different kind of wave, one that needs no medium, and it is the subject of the next section.

You can feel the medium at work on the site's drum bench. Tap a drum and hold a hand a few centimeters from the skin. You feel the puffs of air. Rest a fingertip on the skin instead and the sound dies, because you stopped the vibration that was doing the pushing.

words.d: a wave that travels by pushing particles of a medium against each other; sound is one
a region in a sound wave where particles are squeezed closer together
a space with no matter in it, not even air

look.title: Boyle's Bell in the Jar
look.text: In his reports on the air pump, Boyle described placing a watch or small bell inside the glass receiver and pumping the air out. As the air was removed, the sound grew faint until it could scarcely be heard, though the mechanism could still be seen moving. When air was let back in, the sound returned.
look.cite: Robert Boyle, experiments with the air pump, about 1660
look.prompt: Why did Boyle need to see the watch still working? What would he have concluded if he had not checked?

check.q: Why does a ringing bell go silent inside a jar with the air pumped out?
choices: The bell stops vibrating in a vacuum
There are no particles to carry the pushes to the glass
check.why: Sound is a mechanical wave and needs a medium. With no air, the vibrations of the bell have nothing to push on.

check.q: Which of these could an astronaut floating outside a spacecraft hear directly through space?
choices: Nothing, because space is a vacuum
check.why: Space has almost no particles, so sound cannot travel through it at any loudness. Radio works because it is not sound.

check.q: What is a compression in a sound wave?
choices: A place where the medium is missing
A place where the wave stops
A place where particles are spread apart
A place where particles are squeezed closer together
check.why: A vibrating object squeezes the air in front of it. That squeezed region, the compression, travels outward as part of the wave.

lessons.title: How Fast Sound Travels
lessons.mainIdea: Sound moves at about 343 meters per second in air, faster in water, and faster still in steel, because stiffer, denser media pass pushes along more quickly.
reading: Watch a lightning flash and start counting. Thunder arrives a few seconds later. The light reached you almost instantly, but the sound crawled along at about 343 meters per second, the *speed of sound* in air at room temperature. Every 3 seconds of delay means the strike was roughly 1 kilometer away. Sound is fast by human standards, but the flash shows you it is not instant.

The speed of sound depends on the medium. In water, sound travels about 1,480 meters per second, more than four times faster than in air. In steel, it races along at nearly 6,000 meters per second. Particles in liquids and solids are packed closer and bonded more stiffly, so a push at one end is passed to the far end quickly. Air particles are far apart and must fly across gaps before they bump the next one.

This is why a swimmer hears a clank underwater before a friend on the dock does. It is also why old stories tell of people pressing an ear to a rail to hear a distant train. Temperature matters too. Warm air carries sound a little faster than cold air. Its particles are already moving faster, so they pass the push along sooner.

words.d: how fast a sound wave travels through a medium; about 343 m/s in air at room temperature
one of the tiny pieces, such as atoms or molecules, that make up matter

look.title: Speed of Sound in Different Media
look.prompt: Why might a sound cross a swimming pool faster than it crosses a gym of the same length?

check.q: You see lightning and hear thunder 6 seconds later. About how far away was the strike?
check.why: Sound covers about 343 meters each second, so 3 seconds is roughly 1 kilometer and 6 seconds is roughly 2 kilometers.

check.q: In which medium does sound travel fastest?
check.why: Steel particles are tightly packed and stiffly bonded, so they pass each push along quickly. Sound does not travel in a vacuum at all.

check.q: Why does sound travel faster in water than in air?
choices: Sound waves are bigger in water
Water particles are closer together and pass pushes along faster
check.why: In a liquid the particles are packed close and each push reaches the next particle sooner. In air, particles must cross gaps first.

lessons.title: How the Ear Hears
lessons.mainIdea: The ear turns air pressure waves into vibrations of the eardrum, then into nerve signals inside the cochlea.
reading: A sound wave that reaches your head is a train of tiny pressure changes in the air. The outer ear funnels them down a short canal to the *eardrum*, a thin skin about the size of a fingernail. Each compression pushes the eardrum in; each stretch lets it spring out. The eardrum vibrates at the same frequency as the sound, thousands of times a second for a high note.

Behind the eardrum sit three tiny bones, the smallest in the body. They work like a lever, passing the vibration to a snail-shaped tube called the *cochlea*, which is filled with fluid. Inside, thousands of hair cells sit along a membrane that is stiff at one end and floppy at the other. High-frequency vibrations shake the stiff end, low ones the far end. Each hair cell fires a nerve signal when its part of the membrane moves, so the brain learns the pitch from which cells are firing.

Loudness is measured in *decibels* (dB). A whisper is about 30 dB, normal talk about 60 dB, and a loud concert can pass 110 dB. Very loud sound bends the hair cells too far and can break them. Unlike skin, they do not grow back. That is why hearing protection matters near power tools and why doctors warn about turning earbuds all the way up.

words.d: a thin membrane in the ear that vibrates when sound waves hit it
a snail-shaped, fluid-filled tube in the inner ear where vibrations become nerve signals
the unit used to measure how loud a sound is

look.title: How Loud Is It?
look.cite: approximate values, NIOSH and CDC hearing-safety materials
look.prompt: Where on this list do you think hearing damage becomes possible after long exposure? What could a worker do about it?

check.q: What does the eardrum do when a sound wave reaches it?
choices: It absorbs the sound and turns it into heat
It sends the sound wave back out of the ear
It stays still while the bones move
It vibrates at the same frequency as the sound
check.why: The pressure changes in the wave push and release the eardrum, so it vibrates in step with the sound.

check.q: How does the brain tell a high note from a low note?
choices: Different hair cells along the cochlea fire for different frequencies
The eardrum vibrates louder for high notes
The three bones move only for low notes
The outer ear folds change shape
check.why: The membrane in the cochlea responds to high frequencies near one end and low frequencies near the other. Which hair cells fire tells the brain the pitch.

check.q: Why can very loud sound cause permanent hearing loss?
choices: Hair cells in the cochlea can break and do not regrow
Loud sound travels faster and skips the ear
check.why: Loud sounds bend the hair cells too far. Broken hair cells are not replaced, so the loss can be permanent.

lessons.title: Light Needs No Medium
lessons.mainIdea: Light is a wave that can cross empty space and travels about 300,000 kilometers per second, far faster than sound.
reading: Sunlight crosses about 150 million kilometers of nearly empty space to reach Earth. Sound could never make that trip; it needs particles to push. Light does not. It is an *electromagnetic wave*, a traveling pattern of electric and magnetic fields that carries its own energy along without a medium. In empty space it moves at about 300,000 kilometers per second, the fastest anything can travel.

That speed is so great that light seems instant on Earth. Flip a switch and the room is lit with no delay you can notice. But over big distances the delay shows. Light from the sun takes about 8 minutes to reach us. When you look at the moon, you see it as it was a little over a second ago. The first person to measure this delay was the Danish astronomer Ole Roemer in 1676, who noticed that the eclipses of Jupiter's moon Io ran late when Earth was far from Jupiter and early when it was close.

Light is still a wave, with amplitude, wavelength and frequency. Amplitude shows up as brightness. Wavelength and frequency show up as color. Red light has the longest wavelength the eye can see, about 700 nanometers, and violet the shortest, about 400. A nanometer is one billionth of a meter, so several hundred waves of visible light fit across the width of a single human hair.

words.d: a wave of electric and magnetic fields that carries energy and needs no medium; light is one
one billionth of a meter, used to measure wavelengths of light

look.title: Roemer and the Late Eclipses
look.text: Roemer reported to the French Academy that the moments when Jupiter's moon Io vanished into the planet's shadow did not keep a steady schedule. When Earth was moving away from Jupiter the eclipses came later than predicted, and when Earth was approaching they came earlier. He argued that the difference was the time light needed to cross the extra distance, and that light therefore travels at a finite speed.
look.cite: Ole Roemer, report to the Académie des Sciences, Paris, 1676
look.prompt: Why would eclipses of a moon of Jupiter be a good clock for testing whether light takes time to travel?

check.q: Why can light from the sun reach Earth when sound from the sun cannot?
choices: Light needs no medium; sound cannot cross the near-vacuum of space
Sound is absorbed by the moon
check.why: Light is an electromagnetic wave and carries itself through empty space. Sound is mechanical and needs particles, which space mostly lacks.

check.q: About how long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
check.why: Light covers about 300,000 kilometers each second. The 150 million kilometers to the sun take about 8 minutes.

check.q: For light, what does a change in wavelength show up as to the eye?
check.why: Wavelength and frequency set the color of light. Amplitude sets brightness. Loudness belongs to sound, not light.

lessons.title: Bounce, Soak, Pass Through
lessons.mainIdea: When light meets a material it can reflect, be absorbed, or be transmitted, and the mix decides what we see.
reading: Stand in a sunny room and look around. The mirror shows your face. The black sweater on the chair looks dark and feels warm. The window lets the yard show through. Each object is doing something different with the same sunlight. Light can *reflect*, bouncing off a surface. It can be *absorbed*, its energy taken in and usually turned into heat. Or it can be *transmitted*, passing through. Most objects do a mix of all three.

Reflection follows a simple rule. Light bounces off a smooth surface at the same angle it came in, like a ball off a wall. A mirror is smooth enough to keep the rays in order, so an image forms. A sheet of white paper reflects almost as much light as a mirror. But its surface is bumpy at a tiny scale, so the rays scatter in every direction. That is why paper looks bright but shows no image.

Color comes from which wavelengths get absorbed. A red apple absorbs most of the blue and green in white light and reflects the red. A black shirt absorbs nearly all colors, which is why it warms up faster in sunlight than a white one. A clear window transmits most light, while tinted glass absorbs some wavelengths and transmits the rest. On a hot Chicago afternoon, that is the difference between a car with a black roof and one with a white roof.

words.d: to bounce off a surface
to take in light energy, usually turning it into heat
to let light pass through

look.title: Two Cars in the Sun
look.text: Two cars sit in a parking lot in July. One is black, the other white. After an hour, a student rests a hand on each roof. The black roof is too hot to touch. The white roof is warm but bearable. Both were parked at the same time in the same sun.
look.prompt: Explain the difference using the words reflect and absorb. What color would you choose for a roof in a hot city, and why?

check.q: Why does white paper look bright but not show your reflection like a mirror?
choices: Paper reflects light but scatters it in every direction
Paper transmits the light to the other side
check.why: Paper reflects a lot of light, but its rough surface sends rays off in all directions, so no ordered image forms.

check.q: A green leaf looks green because it:
choices: Reflects green light and absorbs most other colors
check.why: The color we see is the light that comes back to our eyes. The leaf reflects green and absorbs most of the red and blue.

check.q: Which object transmits the most light?
check.why: Transmit means to let light pass through. A clear window does this best. A mirror reflects and a black sweater absorbs.

lessons.title: Refraction: Light Bends
lessons.mainIdea: Light changes speed when it enters a new material, and that change of speed bends its path.
reading: Put a pencil in a glass of water and look from the side. The pencil seems to break at the surface. Nothing happened to the pencil. The light coming from the underwater part bent as it left the water and entered the air. This bending is called *refraction*, and it happens whenever light crosses from one material into another at an angle.

The cause is speed. Light travels slower in water than in air, and slower still in glass. When a beam hits the surface at a slant, one edge of the beam enters the slow material first and is held back while the other edge is still moving fast. The beam swings around, the way a line of marching students turns if the ones on one end slow down. Light entering a slower material bends toward the line straight into the surface; light leaving it bends away.

Refraction is everywhere. It makes a swimming pool look shallower than it is. It splits white light into a rainbow when it passes through a prism, because each color slows by a slightly different amount and so bends by a slightly different angle. Isaac Newton showed this with a prism in a darkened room in the 1660s. And refraction is the whole trick behind a lens, the subject of the next section.

words.d: the bending of light as it passes from one material into another
a wedge of glass that spreads white light into its colors

look.title: Speed of Light in Different Materials
look.prompt: In which material would light bend the most when entering from air? Why is diamond so sparkly compared with glass?

check.q: A pencil in a glass of water looks bent because:
choices: Light bends as it passes from water into air
Light is absorbed by the water
check.why: Light from the underwater part of the pencil changes speed and direction at the surface, so the image appears shifted.

check.q: What is the direct cause of refraction?
choices: Light changes speed when it enters a new material
Light changes color when it enters a new material
check.why: Light slows down or speeds up when it crosses into a new medium. At an angle, that speed change turns the beam.

check.q: Why does a prism separate white light into colors?
choices: The prism adds color to the light
Each color slows by a different amount and bends by a different angle
The prism reflects each color from a different face
check.why: White light contains all the colors. Each wavelength refracts slightly differently in glass, so they spread apart.

lessons.title: The Eye Is a Camera
lessons.mainIdea: The eye's cornea and lens refract light to form an image on the retina, where cells turn light into nerve signals.
reading: Your eye is a ball about 2.4 centimeters across with a window in the front. Light enters through the clear *cornea*, which does most of the bending. Then it passes through the *pupil*, the dark hole in the middle. The pupil widens in dim light and shrinks in bright light. Behind the pupil sits the *lens*, a soft, clear disc that fine-tunes the focus. Together the cornea and lens refract the rays so they meet on the back wall of the eye.

That back wall is the *retina*, a thin layer of light-sensing cells. The image that lands there is upside down and backward, just as in a camera, but the brain flips it without your noticing. Two kinds of cells do the sensing. Rods work in dim light and see only shades of gray. Cones need brighter light and come in three types tuned to different wavelengths, roughly red, green and blue. Mixing their signals gives every color you see.

The lens can change shape. Small muscles around it squeeze it thicker to focus on a near page and let it flatten to focus on a distant sign. That is why your eyes feel tired after a long time reading up close: the muscles have been working the whole time. With age the lens stiffens, which is why many adults past 40 start holding menus at arm's length.

words.d: the clear front surface of the eye that bends most of the incoming light
the opening in the eye that lets light in; it changes size with brightness
a clear, curved piece of material that bends light to focus it
the layer of light-sensing cells at the back of the eye

look.title: From Bright Sun to a Dark Hallway
look.text: A student walks in from a bright sidewalk into a dim school hallway. For a few seconds she can barely see. Then shapes appear, then faces. Later, walking back outside, the sunlight feels painfully bright until her eyes adjust again.
look.prompt: Which part of the eye is changing during those seconds, and why does the change take time in each direction?

check.q: Which part of the eye does most of the bending of incoming light?
check.why: The clear cornea at the front does most of the refraction. The lens behind it fine-tunes the focus.

check.q: What is the image on the retina like compared with the scene?
check.why: Like a camera, the eye's lens forms an inverted image. The brain corrects it so the world looks upright.

check.q: Why do colors fade in very dim light?
choices: Cones need bright light, so only the rods, which see gray, are working
Light has no color in the dark
check.why: Cone cells sense color but need more light. In dim light the rods take over, and rods report only brightness.

lessons.title: Glasses Fix the Focus
lessons.mainIdea: Nearsighted and farsighted eyes focus light in the wrong place, and a lens of the right shape moves the focus onto the retina.
reading: Some eyes are a little too long from front to back. Light from distant objects comes to a focus before it reaches the retina, then spreads out again, so the far-away sign is a blur while a nearby book is sharp. This is *nearsightedness*, and it is common in teenagers. The fix is a *concave* lens, thinner in the middle than at the edges. It spreads the rays slightly apart before they enter the eye, so they meet a little farther back, right on the retina.

Other eyes are a little too short, or their lens has stiffened with age. Light from a near object would come to a focus behind the retina if it could, so the page is blurry while the far sign is clear. This is *farsightedness*. The fix is a *convex* lens, thicker in the middle, which bends the rays inward so they meet sooner. Reading glasses sold at a drugstore are simple convex lenses.

An eye doctor finds the right lens by trial. You look at letters through lens after lens until the blur snaps into focus, and the strength of that lens is written on your prescription. Contact lenses do the same job by sitting directly on the cornea. Laser surgery reshapes the cornea itself to change how strongly it refracts. All three are the same idea: move the focus onto the retina.

words.d: a condition where distant objects look blurry because light focuses in front of the retina
a condition where near objects look blurry because light would focus behind the retina
a lens thinner in the middle than at the edges; it spreads light rays apart
a lens thicker in the middle than at the edges; it brings light rays together

look.title: Back Row, Front Row
look.text: A student in the back row of a classroom in Rockford keeps squinting at the board but reads her worksheet easily. Her grandfather holds the newspaper far from his face and says the print is too small, though he can read street signs across the road.
look.prompt: Which of them is nearsighted and which is farsighted? What shape of lens would help each one, and why?

check.q: In a nearsighted eye, where does light from a distant object come to a focus?
check.why: The eye is slightly too long, so rays meet before the retina and spread out again, blurring distant objects.

check.q: Which lens helps a farsighted person read a book?
check.why: A convex lens brings rays together sooner, moving the focus forward onto the retina.

check.q: A concave lens is used for nearsightedness because it:
choices: Spreads rays apart so they focus farther back
Bends rays inward so they focus sooner
check.why: Spreading the rays slightly apart before they enter the eye pushes the focus back onto the retina.

review.q: A cork floats on a pond as ripples pass. Which statement is true?
choices: The cork travels with the ripples to the shore
The water carries the cork forward one wavelength per ripple
The ripples stop at the cork
The cork bobs in place while energy passes by
review.why: Waves carry energy, not the medium. The cork stays roughly in place and moves up and down.

review.q: Which describes the sound of a loud, low bass note?
review.why: Loud means large amplitude. Low pitch means low frequency and long wavelength.

review.q: A wave on the bench has a frequency of 2 Hz and a wavelength of 0.4 m. Its speed is:
review.why: Speed equals frequency times wavelength: 2 times 0.4 is 0.8 meters per second.

review.q: Which wave can travel through the vacuum of space?
review.why: Light is electromagnetic and needs no medium. The others are mechanical waves and need matter to push.

review.q: You hear thunder 9 seconds after a lightning flash. The strike was about:
review.why: Sound travels about 343 meters per second, so about 1 kilometer every 3 seconds. Nine seconds is about 3 kilometers.

review.q: In the ear, where are vibrations turned into nerve signals?
review.why: Hair cells inside the fluid-filled cochlea fire nerve signals when their part of the membrane moves.

review.q: A blue shirt looks blue in sunlight because it:
choices: Reflects blue light and absorbs the other colors
review.why: The color you see is the light the object sends back. The shirt reflects blue and absorbs most of the rest.

review.q: A student cannot read the board from the back of the room but reads a book fine. Which lens will help?
review.why: She is nearsighted: light focuses in front of the retina. A concave lens spreads the rays so they focus farther back, on the retina.

chapters.title: Light, Lenses and Signals
chapters.bigQuestion: How do people use waves to see what is too small, too far or too dark for the eye, and to send a picture around the world in a second?

story.title: Four New Stars Beside Jupiter
story.kicker: One cold January night in 1610, a tube with two pieces of glass changed what the sky was allowed to be.
paragraphs: On the evening of January 7, 1610, Galileo Galilei climbed to a window in Padua, Italy, and pointed a homemade tube at Jupiter. The tube was a spyglass. Word had come from the Netherlands a year earlier that a lens maker had put two glass lenses in a tube and made distant church towers leap closer. Galileo ground his own lenses, improved the design, and built one that made things look about 20 times larger.

Jupiter itself was a small bright disc. But beside it, in a neat line, sat three tiny points of light that no chart showed. Galileo assumed they were faint background stars. The next night he looked again, and the three points had moved. Stars do not do that. On later nights a fourth appeared, and the four little lights shifted from side to side of Jupiter, sometimes vanishing behind it, always staying near.

By the middle of January he was sure. These were not stars. They were moons circling Jupiter, the way our moon circles Earth. That mattered enormously. Many scholars still taught that everything in the heavens circled Earth. Here were four objects plainly circling something else. Galileo rushed a small book into print that March, and readers across Europe lined up to buy spyglasses of their own.

The instrument that made this possible was nothing but refraction. One lens gathered far more light than a human pupil could and bent it to a focus. A second lens spread that focused light so the eye could inspect it. Two curved pieces of glass, and a whole planet's family came into view. This chapter is about what people have built since: microscopes, telescopes, cameras, fiber cables and radar, all ways of using waves to carry information the unaided senses could never catch.
story.think: Galileo trusted a brand-new instrument over centuries of teaching. What made his observation convincing enough to change minds, and what could a critic have said back?

lessons.title: What a Lens Does
lessons.mainIdea: A convex lens refracts parallel light rays to a focal point, and objects placed near it appear magnified.
reading: Hold a magnifying glass over a sidewalk on a sunny day and slide it up and down. At one height the sunlight collapses into a tiny, painfully bright spot. That spot is the *focal point*, and its distance from the lens is the *focal length*. The lens is convex, thicker in the middle, so every part of it bends the incoming light toward the center. Parallel rays from the sun meet at one place.

Now hold the same lens over a printed page, closer than its focal length. The letters swell. You are looking at a *magnified* image, larger than the object. The rays leaving each letter are bent by the lens so that, when they reach your eye, they seem to come from a much bigger letter farther away. The eye and brain cannot tell the difference between real rays and bent ones, so you see a giant letter.

A fatter lens, with more curve, has a shorter focal length and magnifies more. But it also blurs and colors the edges of the image. Early lens makers fought these flaws for centuries. Wider lenses gather more light. That is why a telescope lens is much bigger than a magnifying glass. The point is not just to enlarge. It is to collect enough dim light from a distant object to see it at all.

words.d: the spot where a lens brings parallel light rays together
the distance from a lens to its focal point
made to look larger than the real object

look.title: The Water Drop Lens
look.text: A student places a single drop of water on a clear plastic sheet and lays it over a page of newsprint. Through the drop, the letters underneath look noticeably bigger. When she flattens the drop by pressing it, the letters shrink back toward normal size.
look.prompt: Why does a round drop of water work as a lens? What about pressing it flat changed the magnification?

check.q: What is the focal point of a convex lens?
choices: The place where parallel rays are brought together
The point where light is absorbed
The edge where light bends most
check.why: A convex lens bends parallel rays inward so they meet at one spot, the focal point.

check.q: Why does a magnifying glass make letters look bigger?
choices: It makes the letters physically larger
It bends the rays so they seem to come from a larger, farther object
It adds light to the page
It reflects the letters back at your eye
check.why: The lens refracts the rays leaving each letter. To the eye, the bent rays appear to come from a bigger letter.

check.q: Why are telescope lenses made much wider than a magnifying glass?
choices: A wider lens gathers more of the faint light from distant objects
Wide lenses do not need to be curved
check.why: Distant objects send very little light. A large lens collects more of it, making faint things bright enough to see.

lessons.title: Inside a Microscope
lessons.mainIdea: A compound microscope uses two lenses in a row, so the magnification of one is multiplied by the magnification of the other.
reading: The site's microscope has two sets of lenses. Nearest the specimen is the *objective* lens, a small, strongly curved lens that sits a few millimeters above the glass slide. It forms a magnified image of the specimen inside the tube. At the top is the *eyepiece*, which you look through. It acts like a magnifying glass on the image the objective already made. Two enlargements in a row multiply: a 10x objective and a 10x eyepiece give 100x.

Light matters as much as glass. A mirror or lamp under the stage sends light up through the thin specimen. What you see is light transmitted through the sample, with dark parts where cells absorb it. That is why a slice must be very thin. It is also why stains are used. A dye that a cell nucleus absorbs turns the nucleus dark and visible.

In 1665 Robert Hooke published a book of drawings made with a two-lens microscope, including a thin slice of cork that looked like rows of tiny boxes. He called them cells. The name stuck to the units of every living thing. A few years later, Antonie van Leeuwenhoek in the Netherlands used single, tiny, very powerful lenses to see living things in pond water that nobody had known were there.

Light microscopes have a hard limit. Visible light has a wavelength of around 500 nanometers, and anything much smaller than that wavelength simply cannot be resolved by light, no matter how good the glass. Seeing viruses or atoms took a different kind of wave, and electron microscopes in the twentieth century supplied it.

words.d: the lens of a microscope or telescope nearest the object, which forms the first image
the lens you look through, which magnifies the image made by the objective
the sample being examined

look.title: Hooke Looks at Cork
look.text: Hooke wrote that when he cut a thin slice of cork with a sharp penknife and placed it under his microscope, he could see that it was full of tiny pores or boxes, which he compared to a honeycomb. He counted them and estimated that more than a thousand million could fit in a cubic inch. He called these little spaces cells.
look.prompt: Hooke was looking at dead cork, not living cells. Why do you think he chose the word cell, and what did he get right and wrong?

check.q: A microscope has a 40x objective and a 10x eyepiece. Its total magnification is:
check.why: The eyepiece magnifies the image the objective already made, so the two numbers multiply: 40 times 10 is 400.

check.q: Why must a specimen for a light microscope be cut very thin?
choices: So light can pass through it to the lens
So it fits under the eyepiece
So the objective does not magnify it too much
check.why: The image is made from light transmitted through the sample. A thick slice blocks the light and shows only a dark blob.

check.q: Why can a light microscope not show an individual virus clearly?
choices: Viruses are smaller than the wavelength of visible light
check.why: Light cannot resolve details much smaller than its own wavelength, about 500 nanometers. Most viruses are far smaller than that.

lessons.title: Telescopes: Lenses vs Mirrors
lessons.mainIdea: Early telescopes used lenses; large modern telescopes use curved mirrors, which can be built far bigger and gather far more light.
reading: Galileo's telescope was a *refractor*: a large lens at the front gathered light and a small lens at the back magnified it. Refractors improved for nearly three centuries. The largest ever put into regular use is at Yerkes Observatory in Williams Bay, Wisconsin, a two-hour drive from Chicago. Its lens, finished in 1897, is 40 inches, about 1 meter, across. Nobody built a bigger one, because a glass lens that large sags under its own weight and blurs.

The answer was a mirror. In 1668 Isaac Newton built a small telescope that used a curved mirror instead of a front lens. A mirror can be supported from behind, so it can be made huge, and it reflects every color to the same focus, avoiding the color fringes that lenses add. Nearly every large telescope since has been a *reflector*. The Hale telescope on Palomar Mountain, California, finished in 1948, has a mirror about 5 meters across.

Two more problems remained: air and daylight. Earth's atmosphere wobbles, making stars twinkle and images shimmer. The Hubble Space Telescope, launched in 1990 with a 2.4-meter mirror, solved both by orbiting above the air. The James Webb Space Telescope, launched on December 25, 2021, carries a 6.5-meter mirror built from 18 gold-coated hexagons that unfolded in space. It sees in infrared, a kind of light explained in the next section.

Chicago has its own place in this story. The Adler Planetarium on the lakefront, opened in 1930, was the first planetarium in the Western Hemisphere. And every telescope, from Galileo's tube to Webb, works on the same two ideas from the last chapter: gather as much light as possible, and bend it to a focus.

words.d: a telescope that gathers light with a large lens
a telescope that gathers light with a curved mirror
the layer of air around Earth, which blurs and dims starlight

look.title: How Wide Is the Light Collector?
look.cite: observatory and NASA published values, rounded
look.prompt: Hubble's mirror is smaller than Hale's, yet Hubble produced sharper pictures. What did Hubble have that Hale did not?

check.q: Why did astronomers stop building larger refracting telescopes after about 1 meter?
choices: Lenses became too expensive to ship
Larger lenses were not allowed by law
A huge glass lens sags under its own weight and blurs the image
Larger lenses gather too much light
check.why: A lens can only be held at its edge. Past about a meter, its own weight bends it out of shape.

check.q: What is the main advantage of a mirror over a lens for a big telescope?
choices: Mirrors are always lighter than air
Mirrors do not need to be curved
A mirror can be supported from behind, so it can be made very large
check.why: Support from behind lets a mirror be huge without sagging, and mirrors also avoid color fringes.

check.q: Why does placing a telescope in orbit improve its images?
choices: It is above the atmosphere, which blurs and dims starlight
It is closer to the stars
Space is warmer than a mountaintop
check.why: Earth's moving air makes images shimmer. Above it, a telescope sees steady, unblurred light.

lessons.title: Light Beyond the Rainbow
lessons.mainIdea: Visible light is only a small slice of a much wider family of electromagnetic waves, discovered one piece at a time.
reading: In 1800 the astronomer William Herschel spread sunlight into a rainbow with a prism and set a thermometer in each color. Red warmed the thermometer more than violet. Then he tried something odd: he moved the thermometer past the red end, into what looked like empty shadow. It got warmer still. Something invisible was arriving there, carrying energy. He had found *infrared* light, light with a wavelength too long for the eye.

A year later Johann Ritter tried the other end. Paper soaked in silver chloride darkens in light. Ritter found it darkened fastest just beyond the violet, where nothing could be seen. That was *ultraviolet*. Over the next century the family kept growing. In 1887 Heinrich Hertz made and detected radio waves in his lab. In 1895 Wilhelm Röntgen found X-rays, which passed through flesh and cast shadows of bone.

All of these are the same kind of wave as visible light. They are electromagnetic waves traveling at the same speed, differing only in wavelength and frequency. Lined up from longest wavelength to shortest, they make the *electromagnetic spectrum*: radio, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays. Visible light, from about 700 down to 400 nanometers, is a thin sliver near the middle. Shorter wavelength means higher frequency and more energy per wave. That is why ultraviolet burns skin and radio waves do not.

words.d: electromagnetic waves with wavelengths a little longer than red light; felt as heat
electromagnetic waves with wavelengths a little shorter than violet light; can burn skin
the whole range of electromagnetic waves, from radio to gamma rays, ordered by wavelength

look.title: Herschel's Thermometer in the Dark
look.text: Herschel described placing thermometers in the different colors of a spectrum cast by a prism and found that the heating increased from violet toward red. Moving a thermometer beyond the red, where no light was visible, he found the temperature rose even more, and he concluded that the sun sends out invisible rays that carry heat.
look.cite: William Herschel, paper read to the Royal Society, 1800
look.prompt: Herschel used a thermometer instead of his eyes as the detector. Why was that choice the key to the discovery?

check.q: How did Herschel find infrared light?
choices: He saw a dark red glow beyond the rainbow
A thermometer placed beyond the red end of a spectrum warmed up
He heard it on a radio
check.why: Infrared is invisible, but it carries energy. The thermometer detected the energy where his eyes saw nothing.

check.q: Which of these has the shortest wavelength?
check.why: The spectrum runs from long radio waves through visible light to short X-rays and gamma rays.

check.q: Why can ultraviolet light burn skin while radio waves cannot?
choices: Radio waves are absorbed by clouds
Ultraviolet has a higher frequency and more energy per wave
check.why: All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed. Shorter wavelength means higher frequency and more energy.

lessons.title: Waves We Use Every Day
lessons.mainIdea: Different parts of the spectrum do different jobs, from radio for broadcasting to X-rays for seeing bones, based on what each wavelength passes through or is absorbed by.
reading: Look around a kitchen and count the spectrum. The radio on the counter picks up FM signals near 100 megahertz, waves about 3 meters long that bend around buildings. The microwave oven fills its box with waves about 12 centimeters long that water absorbs strongly, so the food heats from the water inside it while the dry plate stays cool. The toaster glows with infrared. The overhead lamp gives visible light. Each job uses the wavelength that behaves the right way.

*Radio waves*, the longest, pass through walls and travel far. That makes them ideal for broadcasting and for cell phones, whose signals sit between a few hundred megahertz and a few gigahertz. *Microwaves* are shorter and can be aimed in tight beams, useful for radar and for Wi-Fi. Infrared cameras see warm bodies in the dark, because everything warm gives off infrared. Ultraviolet from the sun tans and burns. Sunscreen absorbs it before the skin does.

*X-rays* pass easily through soft tissue but are absorbed by bone. So a bone casts a shadow on the film or sensor. Gamma rays, the most energetic, come from radioactive atoms and are used in some cancer treatments. Higher-frequency waves carry more energy, so X-rays and gamma rays can damage cells. That is why a dentist steps out of the room and a lead apron covers your chest.

words.d: the longest electromagnetic waves, used for broadcasting and phone signals
electromagnetic waves shorter than radio waves, used for cooking, radar and Wi-Fi
high-energy electromagnetic waves that pass through soft tissue but not bone

look.title: Frequencies of Some Everyday Radio Signals
look.prompt: Which of these signals has the longest wavelength? Why would a long wavelength help a signal reach a radio in a basement?

check.q: Why does a microwave oven heat the food but leave a dry plate cool?
choices: Microwaves are absorbed by water in the food, not by the dry plate
The plate reflects heat back into the food
The food is closer to the light bulb
check.why: The oven's wavelength is chosen because water absorbs it strongly. The plate has no water, so it stays cool.

check.q: Why do bones show up on an X-ray image?
choices: Bones glow when hit by X-rays
Bones absorb X-rays while soft tissue lets them pass
Bones reflect X-rays back to the camera
check.why: X-rays pass through soft tissue but are stopped by dense bone, so bone casts a shadow on the detector.

check.q: Which part of the spectrum lets an infrared camera see a person in complete darkness?
choices: Radio waves from the person's phone
Infrared given off by the warm body
check.why: Anything warm emits infrared. The camera detects that emitted radiation, with no visible light needed.

lessons.title: Seeing in Other Light
lessons.mainIdea: Telescopes that detect infrared, radio or X-rays reveal objects and events that visible light cannot show.
reading: The universe does not shine only in colors we can see. Clouds of dust that block visible light are nearly transparent to infrared. So an infrared telescope can look straight through them at the stars forming inside. The James Webb Space Telescope was built for exactly this. Its mirror is coated in a thin layer of gold, because gold reflects infrared very well. The whole telescope hides behind a sunshield the size of a tennis court, so its own warmth does not blind it.

There is a second reason Webb sees in infrared. The universe is expanding. Light from the most distant galaxies has been stretched during its long trip, shifting visible light into the infrared. Catching that stretched light lets Webb see galaxies as they were more than 13 billion years ago, when the universe was young. A telescope is a kind of time machine. The farther away it looks, the further back in time it sees.

Radio telescopes, huge dish antennas, map cold hydrogen gas and the leftover glow of the early universe. X-ray telescopes in orbit catch the light from gas heated to millions of degrees near black holes. Each window in the spectrum shows a different universe. Astronomers combine them into one picture. A doctor does the same with an X-ray, an ultrasound and a photograph of one patient.

words.d: a set of thin layers that block the sun's heat and light from a space telescope
an enormous group of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity

look.title: NASA on Why Webb Sees Infrared
look.text: NASA explains that Webb observes in infrared for two main reasons. Light from the earliest galaxies has been stretched by the expansion of the universe into infrared wavelengths, so only an infrared telescope can catch it. And infrared passes through the clouds of dust where stars and planets form, letting the telescope see inside regions that hide from visible-light telescopes.
look.cite: NASA, James Webb Space Telescope science overview
look.prompt: Why does Webb need to stay very cold, and how does the sunshield help with that?

check.q: Why is Webb's mirror coated with gold?
choices: Gold reflects infrared light very well
check.why: Webb collects infrared. Gold is an excellent infrared reflector, so the coating sends that light to the detectors.

check.q: Why can an infrared telescope see stars forming inside a dust cloud?
choices: Infrared passes through dust that blocks visible light
Infrared is brighter than visible light
Dust clouds glow in visible light
check.why: Dust grains scatter visible light strongly but let longer infrared waves pass, so the stars inside show through.

check.q: Why is looking at a very distant galaxy also looking into the past?
choices: Distant galaxies move backward in time
Its light took billions of years to arrive, so we see it as it was when the light left
Galaxies stop changing after they form
check.why: Light travels at a fixed speed. Light from a galaxy 13 billion light-years away left it 13 billion years ago.

lessons.title: Analog and Digital
lessons.mainIdea: An analog signal copies a wave's shape directly, while a digital signal turns it into numbers, which resist noise and copy perfectly.
reading: The groove on a vinyl record is an *analog* signal. Its wiggle is a direct copy of the sound wave's shape: twice as loud, twice as wide. That is simple and elegant, but it has a weakness. Every scratch, every speck of dust, every bit of wear adds its own wiggle, and the player cannot tell the added wiggle from the music. Copy an analog tape to another tape and the hiss of the first copy is copied too, plus new hiss. After a few generations the music is buried.

A *digital* signal takes a different route. Thousands of times a second, it measures the wave's height and writes the measurement down as a number. Each number is stored as a string of *bits*, ones and zeros. A CD samples the wave 44,100 times each second. Instead of a shape, the recording is a long list of numbers.

Numbers can be protected in a way shapes cannot. A one is sent as a high voltage or a bright flash, a zero as a low voltage or darkness. Noise may nudge a high signal a little lower or a low signal a little higher, but as long as the receiver can still tell high from low, it reads the bit correctly and the noise vanishes. Extra check bits let the receiver notice and fix bits that did get flipped. A digital file copied a million times is still exactly the same file.

This is why phone calls, streaming music, photographs and this web page are all digital. The trade-off is that a digital recording only keeps what it measured. Sample too rarely or store too few bits per sample and the sound gets coarse. Engineers choose sample rates high enough that the ear cannot tell the difference.

words.d: a signal that copies the shape of the original wave directly
a signal made of numbers, stored as ones and zeros
a single one or zero, the smallest piece of digital information
unwanted random changes added to a signal

look.title: Passing a Message Down a Line
look.text: Two classes play a game. In the first, a student draws a curvy line on paper and each person in a row copies the drawing by hand and passes their copy on. In the second, a student writes the numbers 3, 7, 2, 9 and each person copies the numbers. After twenty copies, the drawings barely resemble the original, but the numbers are still 3, 7, 2, 9.
look.prompt: Which class was passing an analog signal and which a digital one? Why did the numbers survive when the drawing did not?

check.q: What is the main weakness of an analog signal?
choices: Noise gets added and cannot be separated from the signal
It travels more slowly than a digital one
check.why: An analog signal is a shape. Any scratch or hiss changes the shape, and the player cannot tell which wiggle was the original.

check.q: Why can a digital signal ignore small amounts of noise?
choices: Noise cannot touch a digital wire
The receiver only has to tell a high from a low, and small nudges do not change that
check.why: Each bit is either high or low. As long as noise does not push one across to the other, the bit reads correctly and the noise is discarded.

check.q: What is a bit?
choices: One wiggle in a record groove
A small scratch on a disc
check.why: A bit is the smallest unit of digital information: one binary digit, either 1 or 0.

lessons.title: How a Phone Sends a Picture
lessons.mainIdea: A phone turns a picture into millions of numbers, sends them as bits over radio waves and cables, and the receiving phone rebuilds the image from the numbers.
reading: You take a photo of the Bean in Millennium Park and tap send. Inside the camera, a grid of millions of tiny light sensors, one per *pixel*, has measured how much red, green and blue light landed on it. Each color is stored as a number from 0 to 255, so each pixel is three numbers, and each number is 8 bits. A 12-million-pixel picture is nearly 300 million bits before anything else happens.

That is too much to send quickly, so the phone *compresses* the image. It looks for patches where neighboring pixels are nearly the same color, such as the sky, and stores a short description instead of every value. A typical photo shrinks to a few million bits with almost no visible loss. The file is then chopped into packets, each labeled with where it belongs.

The phone's antenna sends the packets as radio waves to a cell tower that may be a kilometer away. The wave is switched on and off, or shifted slightly, to mean one or zero. From the tower the bits usually travel by glass fiber, as pulses of light. They pass through switching centers, possibly across an ocean, to the tower nearest your friend. Her phone receives the radio packets and checks each one for errors. It asks again for any that were damaged, then rebuilds the numbers.

Finally her screen does the reverse of your camera: at each pixel it lights three tiny red, green and blue elements to the strength the numbers say. The whole trip takes about a second, and nothing physical made the journey. Only a pattern did, exactly as with the ripple on the pond in the last chapter.

words.d: one tiny square of a digital image, stored as numbers for red, green and blue
to shrink a file by storing repeated or predictable parts more briefly
a small labeled chunk of a digital message sent separately and reassembled

look.title: The Photo That Arrived Blocky
look.text: A student sends a photo of a sunset over Lake Michigan while riding a train through a tunnel. The picture arrives, but the sky looks like large flat squares instead of a smooth gradient, and a friend asks why it looks so much worse than the original.
look.prompt: The phone chose a stronger compression because the connection was weak. Using what you know about pixels and compression, explain why the sky turned into squares.

check.q: In a digital photo, what is stored for each pixel?
choices: Numbers for how much red, green and blue light was measured
A tiny copy of the whole image
check.why: Each pixel's color is recorded as three numbers, typically 0 to 255 each, for red, green and blue.

check.q: Why does a phone compress a photo before sending it?
choices: To shrink the number of bits so it sends faster
To turn it from digital into analog
check.why: A raw image is hundreds of millions of bits. Compression stores repeated areas briefly, cutting the size many times over.

check.q: Which two carriers usually take the bits between your phone and a distant friend's phone?
choices: Radio waves to the tower, then light pulses in glass fiber
check.why: Phones talk to towers by radio. Between towers and across long distances, the bits ride as light in fiber-optic cables.

lessons.title: Light in a Glass Thread
lessons.mainIdea: Optical fiber traps light inside a hair-thin strand of glass by total internal reflection and carries digital signals across oceans.
reading: Aim a flashlight up from under water at a shallow angle and the light does not leave the pool. It bounces off the surface as if the surface were a mirror. This is *total internal reflection*. Light moving from a slower material such as water or glass toward a faster one such as air is bent away from the surface, and past a certain angle it cannot escape at all. It reflects back in, losing almost nothing.

An *optical fiber* uses this trick on purpose. It is a strand of extremely pure glass thinner than a human hair. It is wrapped in a second glass layer that light travels through faster. Light pulses entering one end glance off the boundary again and again, tens of thousands of times per kilometer. They stay trapped in the core until they come out the far end. A laser flashes on for a one and off for a zero, billions of times each second.

Fiber beats copper wire in every way that matters for signals. The glass is so pure that a pulse can travel 100 kilometers before it needs a boost. A window pane that pure would let you see clearly through a stack a kilometer thick. Light pulses do not interfere with each other the way electric currents in nearby wires do. One fiber can carry many colors at once, each color a separate stream of bits. Undersea fiber cables now carry nearly all international internet traffic. The first was laid across the Atlantic in 1988.

The idea reaches back to 1880. That year Alexander Graham Bell sent a voice a few hundred meters on a beam of sunlight, with a device he called the photophone. Clouds blocked it, so it was never practical. Glass gave the light a protected road. In 1966 the engineer Charles Kao showed that glass pure enough could make that road span the world.

words.d: when light inside a slower material hits the boundary at a shallow angle and reflects completely instead of escaping
a hair-thin strand of very pure glass that carries light signals by trapping them inside
a device that produces a narrow, single-color beam of light

look.title: Bell Hears Sunlight Speak
look.text: In a letter written in 1880, Bell told his father that he had managed to make a beam of sunlight carry his voice. He wrote with excitement that he had heard speech produced by sunlight and had heard a sunbeam laugh, cough and sing, and he thought this photophone might be his greatest invention.
look.cite: Alexander Graham Bell, letter to his father, 1880
look.prompt: Bell's photophone worked but was never widely used. What problem did optical fiber solve that Bell could not?

check.q: What keeps light trapped inside an optical fiber?
choices: Total internal reflection at the boundary of the glass core
A metal coating that absorbs stray light
The light is too slow to escape
check.why: Light hits the boundary between core and outer layer at a shallow angle and reflects fully back inside, over and over.

check.q: How is a one or a zero sent down a fiber?
choices: As a high or low sound
As a flash of light on or off
As a red or blue color
As a thick or thin strand
check.why: A laser turns on for a one and off for a zero, billions of times per second, and the pulses travel through the glass.

check.q: Why can one fiber carry many separate streams of bits at the same time?
choices: The bits travel at different speeds
Different colors of light travel in the same fiber without mixing
Each stream uses a different tower
check.why: Different wavelengths of light do not interfere with one another, so each color can carry its own signal through the same strand.

lessons.title: Sonar and the Bat
lessons.mainIdea: Sonar and echolocation send out sound and time the echo, using the speed of sound to turn delay into distance.
reading: Shout across a canyon and a moment later the canyon shouts back. The delay is the round trip of your sound to the far wall and back. If you know the speed of sound, you can measure the distance without a tape: distance equals speed times time, divided by two because the sound went there and back. A 2-second echo in air means the wall is about 343 meters away.

*Sonar* does this on purpose, under water. A ship sends a sharp click downward and listens. In seawater, sound travels about 1,500 meters per second, so an echo that returns after 4 seconds came from a bottom about 3,000 meters down. Sweeping the click across the seafloor maps mountains and trenches that no one can see. Sonar was developed after the sinking of the Titanic in 1912 and during the First World War to find icebergs and submarines, and it still does both.

Bats invented the method millions of years earlier. A hunting bat squeaks at frequencies up to about 100,000 hertz, far above human hearing, and listens for the echo from a moth. Its calls are high-pitched because short wavelengths bounce off small objects that long waves would pass around. Dolphins do the same with clicks under water. The site's drum bench lets you try a slow version: tap once and listen for the return from the far wall of the room.

*Ultrasound* in a doctor's office is sonar at very small scale. A probe sends pulses into the body and times the echoes from organs and from a baby's heartbeat, building a picture out of nothing but delay. Sound is a safer choice than X-rays for this job because it carries far less energy per wave.

words.d: finding objects under water by sending sound and timing the echo
the way bats and dolphins find things by listening to echoes of their own calls
sound too high for humans to hear, used to make images inside the body

look.title: Sonar Echo Time and Depth
look.cite: calculated from about 1,500 m/s in seawater, rounded
look.prompt: Why is the depth for each row half of the speed times the time? What would go wrong if the water were much warmer than expected?

check.q: A ship's sonar ping returns after 2 seconds. With sound at about 1,500 m/s in seawater, how deep is the bottom?
check.why: The sound went down and back, so divide the round trip by two: 1,500 times 2 seconds is 3,000 meters there and back, or 1,500 meters deep.

check.q: Why do bats use very high-frequency calls for echolocation?
choices: Short wavelengths bounce off small prey like moths
check.why: A wave tends to pass around objects smaller than its wavelength. Short, high-frequency waves reflect from small insects.

check.q: Why is ultrasound rather than X-rays used to look at a baby before birth?
choices: Sound waves carry far less energy per wave than X-rays and do not damage cells
check.why: X-rays are high-energy and can harm cells. Ultrasound builds a picture from gentle echoes.

lessons.title: Radar and the Weather Map
lessons.mainIdea: Radar sends radio waves and times the echo, and the tiny frequency shift of a moving target reveals its speed, which is how weather radar tracks storms.
reading: *Radar* is sonar with radio waves. A dish sends a pulse of microwaves and listens for the reflection. Because the waves travel at the speed of light, the timing is fierce: an echo from an airplane 15 kilometers away returns in one ten-thousandth of a second. Electronics measure that easily, and a rotating dish turns the delays into dots on a screen. Radar was developed in Britain and the United States during the 1930s, and by 1940 it was warning of approaching aircraft.

Raindrops reflect microwaves too. Weather radar sends pulses into the sky and paints a map of where rain and hail are, colored by how strong the echo is. Watch a Chicago forecast and the green, yellow and red blotches sliding across Illinois are radar echoes, updated every few minutes.

Modern weather radar does something more. When a wave reflects from an object moving toward the dish, the returning wave is squeezed to a slightly higher frequency. From an object moving away, it is stretched lower. This is the *Doppler effect*, the same reason a passing siren drops in pitch. By measuring the shift, Doppler radar sees which way the rain is moving inside a storm. A patch of echoes rushing toward the dish right beside a patch rushing away means a rotating column. That is a possible tornado, and the warning goes out before the funnel touches down.

Every technology in this unit is the same idea wearing different clothes. Send a wave, or catch one that is already there. Measure its amplitude, its timing, its frequency. Turn the measurements into information. The turntable does it with a groove, the eye with a lens, the bat with a squeak and the weather service with a spinning dish.

words.d: finding objects by sending radio waves and timing the echo
the change in frequency of a wave when its source or reflector is moving toward or away from you

look.title: The Siren on Lake Shore Drive
look.text: An ambulance races past a student waiting at a crosswalk. As it approaches, the siren sounds high and urgent. The instant it passes, the pitch drops, though the driver never touched the siren. A weather radar in the suburbs uses the very same effect to see wind inside a thunderstorm.
look.prompt: Explain what happens to the sound waves reaching the student as the ambulance approaches and then moves away. How does radar use this to spot a rotating storm?

check.q: What does weather radar actually detect when it shows rain on a map?
choices: Microwave echoes reflected from raindrops and hail
check.why: The radar sends microwave pulses and records where they bounce back. Raindrops reflect them, and stronger echoes mean heavier rain.

check.q: A reflected wave returns at a higher frequency than it was sent. What does that tell the radar?
choices: The object is very far away
The object is made of metal
The object is moving toward the radar
check.why: Motion toward the dish squeezes the returning waves to a higher frequency. That is the Doppler effect.

check.q: Why can radar measure distances to aircraft while sonar is used for the sea floor?
choices: Radio waves travel through air but sound works better in water, and each is matched to its medium
Radio waves cannot travel through air
check.why: Radio waves are strongly absorbed by seawater but travel freely through air. Sound travels well through water. Each tool uses the wave that survives the trip.

review.q: In a compound microscope, what is the job of the objective lens?
choices: To reflect light to the eyepiece
To form the first magnified image of the specimen
review.why: The objective, nearest the specimen, makes a magnified image inside the tube. The eyepiece then magnifies that image again.

review.q: Why are the largest telescopes reflectors rather than refractors?
choices: A mirror can be supported from behind and made very large without sagging
Mirrors are more transparent than lenses
Reflectors do not need to be pointed
review.why: A lens can only be held at its edge and bends under its own weight past about a meter. A mirror can be huge.

review.q: Which lists the electromagnetic spectrum from longest wavelength to shortest?
review.why: Radio waves are the longest, then infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and finally gamma rays.

review.q: The Webb telescope observes in infrared partly because:
choices: Infrared is the brightest kind of light
Its mirror cannot reflect visible light
Light from the most distant galaxies has been stretched into the infrared
Infrared travels faster than visible light
review.why: The expansion of the universe stretches the light of early galaxies to longer wavelengths, into the infrared.

review.q: A digital signal resists noise better than an analog one because:
choices: The receiver only needs to tell high from low, so small noise is ignored
review.why: Bits are ones and zeros. Noise that does not flip a bit is simply discarded, and check bits catch flips that do happen.

review.q: Which happens first when a phone sends a photo?
choices: The camera measures red, green and blue light at each pixel and stores numbers
The picture is sent as light through a fiber
The friend's screen lights up its pixels
The cell tower forwards the packets
review.why: The image must be turned into numbers before it can be compressed, packaged and transmitted.

review.q: What keeps a light pulse inside an optical fiber over many kilometers?
choices: Total internal reflection at the boundary of the core
The pulse is too weak to leave
review.why: Light in the glass core strikes the boundary at a shallow angle and reflects completely back in, again and again.

review.q: A sonar echo returns after 6 seconds in seawater at about 1,500 m/s. How deep is the bottom?
review.why: The round trip is 1,500 times 6, or 9,000 meters. The sound went down and back, so the depth is half: 4,500 meters.
